Mixed Effects Multilevel Models

Author

Andreas Haupt

Let’s get ready

Re-scaled weights (Snijders and Bosker 2012, Ch. 14)

Within and between variation

  • We have 29 clusters (groups or macro units) indexed by \(j ( = 1, ..., N)\).
  • The individuals (micro units) are embedded in these clusters, and indexed by \(i ( = 1, ..., n_{j})\).
  • Xenophobia is the dependent variable and varies across individuals and clusters: \(Y_{ij}\).
  • Plot
  • Code

Do party positions predict how people think about immigration?

. . .

But that would be wrong!

One of the critical OLS assumptions is the independence of errors, after all predictors \(x_{ij}\) have been taken into account:

\[\text{Cov}(\epsilon_{i}, \epsilon_{i'} | x_{ij}) = 0\] Breaching this assumptions does not bias \(\beta\) estimates. But it renders them less precise and statistical inference as overoptimistic (i.e., standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values will be too small, and t-values too large).

Understanding the problem

In this simulated example, it is easily visible that the errors of respondents belonging to the same cluster \(j\) are correlated: \(\text{Cov}(\epsilon_{ij}, \epsilon_{i'j}|x_{ij}) \neq 0\). In consequence, the conventional OLS standard error will be too small, by a factor of:

\[\tau \simeq 1 + \rho_{x}\rho_{u}(\bar{N_{g}}-1),\] ::: {.note} where \(\rho_{u}\) is the within-cluster error correlation, \(\rho_{x}\) is the within-cluster correlation of predictor \(x\), and \(\bar{N_{g}}\) is the number of observations per cluster (Cameron and Miller 2015).

This means, statistical inference will be increasingly overoptimistic:

  1. The more of remaining variation in \(y_{ij}\) (i.e., \(e_{ij}\) ) varies across clusters.
  2. The less a predictor \(x_{ij}\) varies within clusters.

Consider our Manifesto variables: They are country-level characteristics and do not very-within out clusters at all; thus they should be badly affected.

:::

Solving the problem The mixed model solution

Micro-level model

We start with a micro-level model, which acknowledges that the intercept varies by cluster:

\[Y_{ij} = \beta_{0 \color{red}{j}} + \beta_{1} x_{1ij} + R_{ij}.\] ::: {.note} - \(\beta_{0j}\) are cluster-differences in the average level of the outcome, adjusted for composition effects of the micro-level predictor(s) \(x_{1ij}\). - \(x_{1ij}\) is any micro-level predictor along with it’s slope coefficient \(\beta_{1}\). \(\beta_{1}\) has no subscript \(j\), which indicates that \(\beta_{1}\) is fixed across clusters. - \(R_{ij}\) are common random unexplained residuals, with \(R_{ij} = \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\).

Source: (Snijders and Bosker 2012, 45)

:::

Solving the problem The mixed model solution

Micro-level model

We start with a micro-level model, which acknowledges that the intercept varies by cluster:

\[Y_{ij} = \beta_{0 \color{red}{j}} + \beta_{1} x_{1ij} + R_{ij}.\] ::: {.note} - \(\beta_{0j}\) are cluster-differences in the average level of the outcome, adjusted for composition effects of the micro-level predictor(s) \(x_{1ij}\). - \(x_{1ij}\) is any micro-level predictor along with it’s slope coefficient \(\beta_{1}\). \(\beta_{1}\) has no subscript \(j\), which indicates that \(\beta_{1}\) is fixed across clusters. - \(R_{ij}\) are common random unexplained residuals, with \(R_{ij} = \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)\).

:::

Mixed (random intercept) multilevel models

Micro-level model

We start with a micro-level model, which acknowledges that the intercept varies by cluster:

\[Y_{ij} = \beta_{0 \color{red}{j}} + \beta_{1} x_{1ij} + R_{ij}.\]

Macro-level model

We continue with a macro-level model that takes the varying intercepts as outcome variable:

\[\beta_{0 \color{red}{j}} = \gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1} z_{1j} + U_{j}.\] ::: {.note} - \(\gamma_{0}\) is the overall mean intercept. - \(z_{1j}\) is a macro-level predictor along with its slope coefficient \(\gamma_{01}\). - \(U_{j}\) are random unexplained group residuals, with \(U_{j} = \mathcal{N}(0,\tau_{0}^2)\). That is, the cluster-specific deviations from \(\gamma_{0}\).

:::

Mixed (random intercept) multilevel models

Random intercept model

\[Y_{ij} = \underbrace{\gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01} z_{1j} + \gamma_{10} x_{1ij}}_{\text{Fixed part}} + \underbrace{U_{0j} + R_{ij}}_{\text{Random part}}.\]

  • Fixed part: The slopes of explanatory micro- and macro-level variables and the overall intercept. These are non-varying point estimates and thus called “fixed.”
  • Random part: \(U_{0j}\) and \(R_{ij}\) are assumed to be normally-distributed random variables that are generated by unmeasured processes. They are leftover macro- and micro-level residuals. As random variables, their concrete values remain latent. We therefore only estimate their variances: \[\begin{align*} \text{var}(U_{0j}|X) &= \tau_{0}^2 \text{ (leftover between-cluster variation)}, \\ \text{var}(R_{ij}|X) &= \sigma^2 \text{ (leftover within-cluster variation)}.\\ \end{align*}\]

Mixed (random intercept) multilevel models

Random intercept model

\[Y_{ij} = \underbrace{\gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01} z_{1j} + \gamma_{10} x_{1ij}}_{\text{Fixed part}} + \underbrace{U_{0j} + R_{ij}}_{\text{Random part}}.\]

  • Fixed part: The slopes of explanatory micro- and macro-level variables and the overall intercept. These are non-varying point estimates and thus called “fixed.”
  • Random part: \(U_{0j}\) and \(R_{ij}\) are assumed to be normally-distributed random variables that are generated by unmeasured processes. They are leftover macro- and micro-level residuals. As random variables, their concrete values remain latent. We therefore only estimate their variances: \[\begin{align*} \text{var}(U_{0j}|X) &= \tau_{0}^2 \text{ (leftover between-cluster variation)}, \\ \text{var}(R_{ij}|X) &= \sigma^2 \text{ (leftover within-cluster variation)}.\\ \end{align*}\]

Source: Bristol Centre for Multilevel Modelling

Further advanced topics

  1. Beware that mixed (random intercept) models don’t work perfectly well if you have less than 30 clusters. Elff et al. (2020) discuss the problems in detail.
  2. Interaction effects between a micro-level variable (e.g., education) and a macro-level characteristic are called cross-level interactions. They actually requite a more complex type of mixed (random intercept and slope model). Heisig and Schaeffer (2019) discuss these models and how to estimate them correctly in detail.

Logistic mixed effects models

The upper-level equation is a simple linear model, but its outcome is \(\text{logit}(\alpha_{j})\)!

\[\begin{align*} y_{ij} &= \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_{0j} + \beta x_{ij})}}, \\ \beta_{0j} &= \gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01} z_{j} + U_{j}, \\ y_{ij} &= \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\gamma_{00} + \gamma_{01} z_{j} + \gamma_{10} x_{ij} + U_{j})}}. \end{align*}\]

Logistic mixed models in R

Today’s (important) functions

  1. lmer(): Estimate linear mixed effects (multilevel) regression models.
  2. glmer(): Estimate generalized (non-)linear mixed effects (multilevel) regression models for binary, count, or other categorical data.

Literatur

Cameron, A. Colin, and Douglas L. Miller. 2015. “A Practitioner’s Guide to Cluster-Robust Inference.” Journal of Human Resources 50 (2): 317–72. https://doi.org/10.3368/jhr.50.2.317.
Elff, Martin, Jan Paul Heisig, Merlin Schaeffer, and Susumu Shikano. 2020. “Multilevel Analysis with Few Clusters: Improving Likelihood-Based Methods to Provide Unbiased Estimates and Accurate Inference.” British Journal of Political Science, 1–15. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0007123419000097.
Heisig, Jan Paul, and Merlin Schaeffer. 2019. “Why You Should Always Include a Random Slope for the Lower-Level Variable Involved in a Cross-Level Interaction.” European Sociological Review 35 (2): 258–79. https://doi.org/10.1093/esr/jcy053.
Snijders, Tom A. B., and Roel J. Bosker. 2012. Multilevel Analysis: An Introduction to Basic and Advanced Multilevel Modeling. London: Sage.
